data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism conflates two concepts Popper explicitly kept separate: corroboration (backward-looking report of test-survival) and verisimilitude (forward-looking closeness to truth). The mechanism states that withstanding tests 'increases A's standing as a candidate for containing more truth-content (verisimilitude) relative to B.' This inference—from past corroboration to greater truth-content—is precisely the inductive step Popper's entire philosophy was designed to reject. In 'The Logic of Scientific Discovery,' Popper insists that degree of corroboration is not a measure of anything; it merely reports how severely a theory has been tested. Popper never claimed that corroboration raises verisimilitude standing; doing so would require the assumption that past test-performance is a guide to truth-likeness, which is induction. Therefore the target's claim that its mechanism is 'defensible on Popper's own terms as a non-inductive, critical selection mechanism based on verisimilitude' is internally contradictory: the mechanism it actually describes is inductive by Popper's own definition. This is distinct from the prior Tichý/Miller objection (which concerns whether verisimilitude comparisons are mathematically coherent); the fault here is that even granting verisimilitude is definable, the bridge from corroboration to verisimilitude that the target erects is the very induction Popper repudiated, making the 'on his own terms' defense a misattribution.
